newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Jewish leader is winner in Frankfurt vote.
newsitem.headline: German Jewish leader is winner in Frankfurt vote.

text.p: Germany's Jewish leader Ignatz Bubis was feted as the real winner of a local election in Frankfurt on Sunday after helping his liberal Free Democrats (FDP) enter the city parliament for the first time in 16 years.

Bubis, a Holocaust survivor, helped boost the FDP's share of the vote beyond five percent -- the required minimum to get elected -- while the far right Republicans he vigorously campaigned against slipped to 6.2 percent from 9.3 percent.
Bubis, 70, was the top candidate for the FDP in Germany's financial capital. His gains contrast sharply with a general drop in FDP support elsewhere in local elections throughout the state of Hesse.
"Our first goal has been reached, we're in the Frankfurt parliament. We didn't reach our second aim which was to keep the Republicans out...You can't have everything," Bubis told German television.
He called on Frankfurt to form a government in which all democratic parties were represented. That was the only way to prevent the Republicans becoming a political force in the city.
For many Germans Bubis has become a household name and a figure of moral authority since he became the leader of Germany's 50,000-strong Jewish community in 1992.
His opponents on Sunday readily acknowledged his success. "The Bubis effect came through here," Joschka Fischer, leader of Germany's environmentalist Greens, told German television.

The FDP, junior coalition partners to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) in the Bonn government, gained 5.6 percent of the vote in Frankfurt according to official results, up from 4.4 percent in the last vote in 1993.

By contrast, projections showed that in the state of Hesse overall, support for the FDP melted to 4.0 percent from 5.1 percent as the large parties, the CDU and the Social Democrats (SPD), recorded slight gains.

The vote in Hesse, one of Germany's wealthiest states with 4.5 million eligible voters, was dominated by local issues but carried national implications because it is one of only two elections this year. Hamburg voters cast ballots in September.
Throughout the campaign Bubis rejected the notion put forward by the SPD and CDU that the election should reflect national political issues like unemployment and tax reform.

Nevertheless, the election gave Kohl's CDU a much-needed boost at a time when his government is presiding over the worst unemployment since Adolf Hitler came to power. The CDU in Hesse rose 1.3 points to 33.3 percent.
The CDU's gains were particularly impressive in Frankfurt, where it rose 2.9 points to 36.3 percent.
Bubis, who describes himself as "a German citizen of the Jewish faith", has been credited with drawing a clear distinction between Nazi Germany and contemporary Germany.
He became an outspoken critic of attacks on foreigners and asylum seekers and anti-Semitism during a wave of neo-Nazi violence after German unification in 1990.
Anti-foreigner feeling at the time helped the Republicans gain 9.3 percent of the vote in Frankfurt in 1993.
Born in what is now Wroclaw, Poland, Bubis lost his father, a brother and a sister in Nazi massacres. He worked in a forced-labour camp in Poland until the war ended in 1945.
